title: The cut-off docks
scenario: A storm cut some routes: which stops can still reach each other? The routes here run both ways. How many separate networks do the stops form?

intro.job: A storm cut some routes: which stops can still reach each other? The routes here run both ways. How many separate networks do the stops form?

idea.rule: One walk finds one network — a fresh walk from an unseen stop is a new network.
idea.detail: Same question as Separate networks, after a storm. Every route runs both ways, so the stops fall into networks: groups joined by routes and cut off from each other. One walk from a stop reaches its whole network and nothing else. To count the networks, look at every stop in turn. Any stop no walk has reached yet starts a fresh walk — and every fresh walk is one more network.

model_restatement: Say how many separate networks the stops form — two stops are in the same network if routes join them.

clarify.question: What about a stop with no routes at all?
clarify.answer: It's a network of its own — the shoal and the lighthouse each count as one.

clarify.question: Do the routes run both ways?
clarify.answer: Yes — every route here runs both ways, so a walk from any stop in a network reaches all of it.

clarify.question: Do I count stops or networks?
clarify.answer: Networks — a group of stops joined by routes counts once, however many stops it has.

clarify.question: Where should the first walk start?
clarify.answer: Anywhere — but one walk only finds one network. Every stop no walk has reached yet starts a new one.

clarify_fallback: Good question — assume the simple case.
blueprint: Start at the first stop and walk everywhere its routes lead, remembering each stop you reach. Count the stops you reached.

checkpoints.prompt: Line 3 picks where the walk starts. Which stop is start?

why_line: The draft walks once from the anchor and counts the stops it reaches: 2. It never asks whether the channel, shoal or lighthouse belong to the same network — they don't.

explain.rule: One walk is one sweep of a flashlight: it lights up everything joined to where it starts, and nothing else.
explain.bridge: The walk from the anchor reaches the buoy and stops. What about the channel — who ever starts a walk from there?

fix.rule: Loop over every stop; each one no walk has reached yet starts a fresh walk — and a fresh walk is one more network.

walk.gloss: Look at every stop, not just the first.
Skip stops an earlier walk already reached.
An unreached stop means a new network.
Mark it seen, then walk its whole network.

contrast.wrong_note: counts the stops one walk reached

alternatives.note: The same count with a recursive walk — walk() marks a whole network seen, and the for loop counts how many times it has to start one.

hints: The draft starts one walk from the anchor. Which stops does that walk never reach?
len(seen) counts the stops one walk found, not the networks.
Loop for start in graph; when start is not in seen, count += 1 and walk from it.

follow_up.prompt: A new route joins the buoy to the channel — how many networks now?

checkpoint.prompt: With the buoy joined to the channel, what gets printed?

follow_up.fix_hint: The anchor, buoy and channel are one network now; the shoal, lighthouse and beacon are still alone — 4 in all.

one_liner: One walk finds one network — a fresh walk from an unseen stop is a new network.
